title: Days, Not 4-8 Weeks: Standing Up a Production Integration POC in One Sprint
summary: A day-by-day sprint plan for a working proof-of-concept integration with a system that has no API: success criteria, worked numbers against 4-8 week consultancy quotes, and a one-page business case for your approver.
body_markdown:
The fastest way to get a working proof-of-concept integration with a system that has no API is to build it on a design partner's own account with a vendor that generates direct HTTP endpoints, then wire it into your feature during the same sprint. Integuru builds a sandbox integration in days at no build fee, so a POC fits inside two weeks instead of the 4 to 8 weeks per connector that consultancies typically quote.


You have 14 days until the budget review. The AI feature on your roadmap only works if it can read and write inside a third-party platform with no public API, and the quote in your inbox says 4 to 8 weeks for that one connector. A slide arguing that the integration is feasible will not carry the room, but the feature running against a real account will. What follows is the plan we would hand you.


### **The sprint plan, day by day**


A two-week sprint gives you ten working days. The plan below lands the demo on working day 10 and treats the weekend days in the 14-day window as slack you do not plan on using.

### **Day 1: pick the workflow and the account**


Choose the workflow your demo story needs and nothing else. Include at least one write action, because read-only POCs hide the part that official partner programs usually gate and that your feature probably depends on. Three actions is plenty; the sprint is about proving the path, not covering the platform.


Then pick the design-partner account. Integuru integrations run on a customer's own account with that customer's own credentials, so the partner needs to agree in writing to the POC and enter their login themselves. If the data is health data, ask about a BAA on day 1; Integuru signs them at no extra cost.


The CLI install is the first action, and it takes a few minutes:


` npm install -g integuru`


Run` integuru` with no arguments and it prints a full playbook of the workflow.` integuru login` opens a browser approval, and` integuru platform create` returns a link where the partner enters the platform login in the browser, never in the terminal.


Now choose the build route:


-


**One connector and an engineer who wants hands on it:** use the CLI on the Free plan ($0, 1 platform, 1 account, 100 API calls a month, assisted build-out if needed).


-


**Several connectors, or no spare engineer:** send the list through the[Full Managed Service](https://www.integuru.com/managed-service) . Integuru builds each requested integration for sandbox trial without a separate build fee and typically delivers in a few days.


### **Days 2-4: the sandbox build**


On the CLI route,` integuru integration create` starts a builder run that takes roughly 10 to 20 minutes for a draft. The builder may stop to ask a question about your workflow, and you answer through` integuru integration respond` . The days that follow are for review: test the draft with` integuru integration test --draft` , read the generated documentation, and approve only after the partner has seen the behavior.


On the managed route Integuru does the same work and hands you a sandbox. Either way, spend these days writing the success criteria below into a scorecard, because the build is the short part of this sprint and the proof is the long part.


### **Days 5-8: wire it into the feature**


Treat the integration as an ordinary HTTP endpoint. The CLI's` integuru integration curl` command prints the call: a POST to` https://api.integuru.ai/integrations/invoke` with a bearer API key and a JSON body of` integration_id` ,` account_id` and` input` . Put that behind one adapter function in your codebase, with a timeout, a typed error, and a latency log line. The adapter you write during this sprint is the same one that runs in production, which is the point of building on a real integration instead of a mock.


Keep the AI feature's own logic unchanged during these days. If the feature misbehaves, you want to know whether the cause is your prompt or the integration, and a stable adapter answers that in minutes.


### **Days 9-10: edge cases and load**


Run the criteria below against the partner account and write down every failure. The[edge cases post](https://www.integuru.com/blog/edge-cases-production-account-states) explains why account state is where integrations usually fail.


Load needs a caveat. The Free plan's 100 calls a month covers functional testing but not a load run. For load, ask for the sandbox call allowance in your scoping conversation, or take one month of the Production plan. Do not assume a number nobody has confirmed.


### **POC success criteria**


Agree these on day 1 and score them on day 10. Each one has a pass line, so the demo cannot be argued with.


-


**Write actions succeed.** Every in-scope write completes on the partner account and the change is visible in the platform's own UI. Run each write at least 20 times (our suggested floor) and record the failures.


-


**Latency under target.** Set the number on day 1. Integuru's published figure is sub-3-second responses, so a target of 3 seconds at p95 is a fair test. Measure it from your own service, not from a vendor dashboard.


-


**Account-state edge cases.** Test at least three states, for example an empty account, a populated one, and a user with restricted permissions. A state the integration does not support should return a clear error, never a plausible wrong answer.


-


**Auth renewal.** Expire the session on purpose in the middle of a run and confirm calls recover. If the account uses 2FA, test that path too. Auth auto-healing ships with the Production and managed plans, so ask exactly what the sandbox covers.


-


**Documented schemas.** Every action has written request and response formats in your repo, and an engineer who did not build the POC can call it without asking anyone.

Scale is the other number your approver will ask about. Integuru's site states 10,000,000+ API calls a month across its customers, so the CFO can see the service already runs at volume.

Choose a consultancy when the target is a thick desktop client or an on-premises system, when you want to own and operate every line of code, or when the work is mostly bespoke business logic. Choose managed generation when the target is an authenticated web platform and the cost you worry about is calendar time and upkeep. The trade you accept with managed generation is dependency on Integuru for the integration layer, so ask about continuity terms and read the[trust page](https://www.integuru.com/trust) before you sign. The[buyer's checklist](https://www.integuru.com/blog/evaluate-api-generation-service-production) lists the questions worth asking any provider.


### **The one-page business case**


The champion takes this to the CFO. Fill every line with a number from the sprint, and keep it to one page.


-


**Decision requested:** the budget and the date, in one sentence.


-


**Problem:** the feature that depends on this integration, the revenue or retention it affects, and what the official partner route quoted for time.


-


**POC result:** your day-10 scorecard, with write success rate, p95 latency, states tested and the auth renewal result.


-


**Options compared:** wait for the partner program, hire a consultancy, build in-house, or use managed API generation, each with weeks to production.


-


**Cost:** the POC build fee (none for the sandbox), then monthly cost at your connector and account count, plus the maintenance hours you avoid.


-


**Risks and mitigation:** dependence on a provider, terms of service, data handling and SLA terms, each with a specific answer.


-


**The ask:** connectors in phase one, the owner, and the review date.


Attach a screen recording of the live write action and the scorecard. A recording of a real write on a real account answers most of the questions that a feasibility memo invites. In the review, the line that used to read "waiting on the[partner program](https://www.integuru.com/blog/developers-guide-api-access-any-website) " becomes a working feature and a price, and nobody has to take your word for it.


### **What carries from POC to production**


The integration you tested in the sandbox is the integration that goes live; nothing is rebuilt. Your adapter, your scorecard and your documentation carry over unchanged. What changes is the layer around it: 24/7 on-call maintenance starts, auth auto-healing applies, and the plan moves to Production (from $499 a month) or to the Fully Managed Service on custom pricing, where SLAs are available.


Three things do not carry over automatically: call volume, load profile, and SLA terms. Re-scope all three when you move to production, because a POC sized at 100 calls a month says nothing about a rollout to thousands of end customers. The[pillar guide on connecting software without an API](https://www.integuru.com/blog/how-to-connect-software-without-apis) compares the other routes if you want the full option set first.


### **FAQ**


**What is the fastest way to stand up a POC integration with a no-API system in one sprint?**


Build a sandbox integration on a design partner's own account with a service that generates direct HTTP endpoints, then wire it into your feature during the same sprint. Integuru builds sandbox integrations in days with no build fee, which leaves most of a ten-day sprint for wiring, testing and a live demo.


**How much does an Integuru POC cost?**


The sandbox build carries no separate build fee. The Free plan is $0 a month for 1 platform, 1 account and 100 API calls, and Full Managed Service sandbox builds are free to try. Production starts at $499 a month and includes 24/7 on-call maintenance and auth auto-healing.


**Is an iPaaS like Workato faster than a consultancy for a system with no API?**


It depends on the target. Workato's documentation describes its connector SDK as built for applications with APIs, and for applications without one it points to RPA (user-interface automation), file import, or a database connection. If the system has a web interface but no API, direct HTTP generation is a different route to compare.


**Is the POC code the production code?**


The integration is the same one, so the sandbox work carries into production, followed by 24/7 on-call maintenance. Your own adapter code carries over too. Call volume limits, load profile and any SLA need re-scoping at that point.


**Is it allowed to integrate this way?**


Integuru integrations run on the customer's own account with the customer's own credentials, with the account holder's consent, and never reuse one customer's credentials for another. Terms of service still vary by platform, so read the[plain-language legal guide](https://www.integuru.com/blog/reverse-engineering-private-api-legal) and the trust page, and get the partner's written agreement on day 1.
